extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in scientific misconduct, bioethics, and stem cell research
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedia entry recounting the Hwang Woo-suk cloning/stem-cell scandal, describing the events, ethical issues, investigations, and aftermath; useful as a case study of research misconduct and bioethics reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data integrity / no fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Seoul National University investigation found that both the 2004 and 2005 papers contained fabricated results; Hwang publicly confessed in January 2006 that the research papers were based on fabricated data. Science immediately retracted the two papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research must not contain fabricated or falsified data. Anti-patterns include publishing results later found to be invented or manipulated; consequences shown include institutional investigation, retraction, public confession, loss of position, and criminal prosecution. Maintain raw data, allow independent verification, and subject results to peer review before publicizing extraordinary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent sourcing of human biological materials (oocytes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The eggs, reportedly from several voluntary donors, were in fact from Hwang's two researchers, which Hwang later denied. Disclosure of the real source of oocytes led to immediate ethical controversy and collaborators breaking ties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always disclose the true source of human biological materials. Do not misrepresent donors' identities or relationships to the research team. Anti-patterns: hiding that donors are lab staff or team members, which raises concerns about coercion and invalid consent and can prompt collaborators to sever relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed consent and voluntary donation
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2005 report explicitly stated: 'Patients voluntarily donated oocytes and somatic cells for therapeutic cloning research and relevant applications but not for reproductive cloning ... no financial reimbursement in any form was paid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure donors give informed, voluntary consent for specified uses; document consent and any terms (e.g., no financial reimbursement). Avoid coercion, especially when recruiting subordinates or vulnerable people. Clarify permitted uses (therapeutic vs reproductive) and obtain approvals consistent with consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with bioethics and biosafety laws
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time South Korea was developing its 'Bioethics and Biosafety Act' which proscribed human reproductive cloning and experimental fusion of human and animal embryos; even therapeutic cloning for diseases would require authorised approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers must follow relevant national and local bioethics and biosafety legislation and obtain any required authorizations. Do not undertake activities explicitly prohibited by law (e.g., reproductive cloning where banned). Seek legal and regulatory clearance before initiating ethically sensitive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional review board (IRB) approval and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to the scandal, South Korea implemented a series of research ethics reforms, including stricter institutional review board (IRB) procedures and national guidelines for ethical research practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain IRB/ethics committee approval for human-subjects or human-materials research; follow IRB protocols and reporting requirements. Strengthened IRB procedures are an expected check on consent, donor protection, and study design. Lack of appropriate IRB oversight is an anti-pattern that enables misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and independent verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to parthenogenesis and other groups' failed attempts at primate cloning underscored alternative biological explanations and the need to verify the claimed results. Other labs (e.g., Advanced Cell Technology, failed rhesus attempts) provided context that raised skepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary experimental claims require independent replication and careful exclusion of alternative explanations (e.g., parthenogenetic origin of cells). Provide sufficient methodological detail and materials to allow others to reproduce results; independent verification helps detect errors or fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship, collaborator disclosure and shared responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Gerald Schatten broke ties with Hwang when he learned of the real source of oocytes; controversies about collaborators' knowledge and roles featured prominently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and collaborators must fully disclose methods, data sources, and their contributions. Co-authors should verify key aspects of the work or explicitly state limits to their knowledge. Failure to disclose material facts to collaborators is an anti-pattern that can result in reputational and professional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding coercion and conflicts in participant recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: The eggs were actually from Hwang's researchers (team members), raising concerns about coercion and ethical recruitment practices for donor material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not recruit donors from populations that may be coerced (e.g., junior staff reporting to investigators). Implement safeguards to ensure voluntary participation, separate recruitment from supervisors, and manage conflicts of interest in recruitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible public communication and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Hwang publicly reported breakthroughs (AAAS meeting, press, and media) and was lionized in media and by government before the scientific claims were fully vetted, contributing to the scandal when allegations arose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making grand public claims before independent peer review and validation. Communicate uncertainties clearly and refrain from using publicity to bypass scientific scrutiny. Overhyping results is an anti-pattern that can amplify damage if findings are later discredited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper data handling and prohibition on undisclosed data reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: A whistleblower informed Science of reuse of data; the journal's probe revealed additional data fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain transparent, auditable data records; do not reuse, duplicate, or manipulate datasets without disclosure and justification. Share raw data when appropriate to enable verification. Undisclosed reuse or manipulation of data is a key indicator of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical considerations around embryo use
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics noted that the method 'ultimately wasted many human embryos' and could enable creation of full human clones; bioethical debate centered on embryo destruction and potential reproductive cloning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ethical implications of creating or destroying embryos, weigh therapeutic benefits against moral concerns, and follow legal/regulatory limits. Obtain ethics approval that specifically addresses embryo handling and clearly communicate the ethical rationale and safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability, investigation, and corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: After allegations, institutional and journal investigations led to retractions, resignation, criminal conviction (embezzlement and bioethical violations), and national reforms in research ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish and follow procedures for investigating allegations of misconduct, issue corrections or retractions when warranted, and pursue legal/administrative remedies as appropriate. Transparent corrective actions and systemic reforms (e.g., improved IRB processes) are expected responses to serious ethical failures.
